speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM LOAN AGREEMENT   WAIVER OF INTEREST ENTITLEMENT
speechtext: Could the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker, now tell the house whether Canada will waive the interest due on December 31, 1956, under the United Kingdom loan of 1946? He made a statement on this question on January 11, in which he intimated that the matter was still under consideration.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM LOAN AGREEMENT   WAIVER OF INTEREST ENTITLEMENT
speechtext: The matter is still under active consideration. As the hon. gentleman knows, the terms of the agreement that afford a possibility of there being waivers do not fit the present situation, and there is under active consideration recommending to parliament an amendment to that agreement.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM LOAN AGREEMENT   WAIVER OF INTEREST ENTITLEMENT
speechtext: Will the Prime Minister assure the house that the government is not waiting until the United States first takes action in the matter?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM LOAN AGREEMENT   WAIVER OF INTEREST ENTITLEMENT
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I can assure the house that this was, at the time, a joint undertaking by the United States and Canada to improve the trading situation of the United Kingdom, and though the arrangement was evidenced by two separate agreements they were tied together, in effect, by terms in each of the two separate agreements. It is my hope an arrangement that will be satisfactory to the United Kingdom authorities will be arrived at both by Canada and the United States.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM LOAN AGREEMENT   WAIVER OF INTEREST ENTITLEMENT
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. Is it not possible for Canada to act alone in this matter, and probably in so doing give impetus to similar action by the United States? I point out to him that on December 6 the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as acting prime minister, said that Canada could act alone. Is that or is it not the fact?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM LOAN AGREEMENT   WAIVER OF INTEREST ENTITLEMENT
speechtext: Canada could act alone, but had Canada acted alone originally the effect upon the economy of the United Kingdom would have been quite insufficient. Canada provided 25 per cent of the loan that was made at that time, and it was felt that the effect of the 100 per cent, namely $5 billion, would be substantial in improving the trading position of the United Kingdom. Canada could act alone, but my information leads me to believe that better results will be achieved by continuing these negotiations that are proceeding at the present time than would be achieved by taking separate action just now. The negotiations are proceeding, and I hope it will not be very long before a satisfactory arrangement agreed to by the three governments will be announced.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
I said "so good". Mr. Speaker, yesterday I spoke somewhat along the line that was suggested by the hon. member for Greenwood when he used the term "truth and beauty". I do not wish to proceed with that subject any further. However, I was somewhat interested in noting two newspaper articles. They were both in the Toronto Globe and Mail. One of them was a picture from Sydney, Australia, depicting a winning design which was called "A joke for a masterpiece". It brought to my mind exactly what we have here today. Does the fact that this council is going to be set up mean it is going to try to set down exactly what culture is and what the government, or let us say the council itself as it will be instituted, decides

the people should have in their best interests in so far as the arts and humanities are concerned?
In that same paper was another heading about Regina's new art gallery. I did not take the time to read all about those two new enterprises in the world today, but I was much interested to find that in Saskatchewan apparently, as well as in other provinces- and I can see the reason for it-they have institutions which have been set up for the promotion of the arts. Certainly we have institutions today which are set up for the purpose of doing just what this Canada Council is apparently being established to do. It makes me wonder why we must have a centralized organization whose main purpose apparently is to do the same thing that is being done by the provinces at this time. I am not opposed to, nor do I suggest for one moment that our government should not set up, a fund to assist the provinces in this work or in this type of work, particularly in the educative field. However, I say that here we are going to have an additional cost of administration which is only going to take away from the needy causes themselves.
I have a few further personal observations to make with respect to this matter. I feel that culture, in order to endure, must be given a place in the hearts and the minds of Canadians. We must exemplify our way of life. It must not be an artificial way of life that might be propounded by a certain group of 19 or by some individuals, as the case might be. I am satisfied that the Canadian people who have clamoured for the setting up of the Canada Council certainly did not have that in mind. It is with a great deal of trepidation that I view the thought that possibly we are going to foist upon our people an organization whose main objective is going to be to see to it that a certain line of culture is promoted.
I believe that the arts today are not in the same need of financial assistance as they were some years ago. I am not denying that there are certain ones, and they are excellent-such as the Stratford theatre and others, the drama festivals included-that need help. The fact is that I am satisfied they do need help. But we have organizations set up whereby they can be helped; and I would prefer that the money be transferred to the provincial governments and be put through in that fashion.
Sometimes persons take objection when one says there is more money available for the arts - than there was heretofore. The proof, Mr. Speaker, lies in the fact that every home today is enjoying the arts in its own way, compared with the situation just a few years

ago. Possibly one out of every three homes in this country enjoys television programs. Through the media of these programs they are subjected to certain forms of artistry. Whether or not it is to their liking is not material. It appears on the screen. They have the opportunity to view some of the finer things that we so often hear of.
This bill calls for an expenditure of some $50 million on the arts and humanities. The purpose behind it, I would say, is possibly the appreciation of the arts. But, Mr. Speaker, our view is wrong in that respect. Canadians should not be told they are spending money to have an appreciation of art. We should be spending money rather in learning the art of appreciation. I find that we can spend hundreds of thousands of dollars and still not be able to appreciate it properly. The very fact that we have paintings worth many thousands of dollars in the national gallery in Ottawa is of no particular value to the rest of Canada unless people can enjoy those paintings. Therein lies the profit; it is learning the art of appreciation.
In my own area we have the Vagabond players who have made themselves quite famous in this country. We have the White Rock players from White Rock, another community, who are likewise well known throughout the whole country. We have established a recreational community within the city of New Westminster which looks after the area as a whole fairly well or at least is beginning to do so. Therein we have the facilities to which this money might be made available. But who is going to decide whether it is the White Rock players, the Vagabond players or the recreational council in New Westminster that is to get this money?
I feel that if culture is going to be directed, it should not be directed from the central government down but that rather it should come from within the souls, the minds and hearts of the individuals in the local communities, and be built up. I believe anything we could do to assist them in achieving that end would be better done through the provincial governments.
We may think of a country such as Russia; and when we think about Russia as such we think of servility. We think of the songs of Russia. I am satisfied that probably every member of this house who is at all familiar with music would say it reminds him of the "Volga Boat Song". We have there an expression of the true culture of these people which has actually come from the soil, from the very hearts and the minds of these particular people and from the work they did. We have there depicted the plodding, the trudging, the heavy work these Russian
Canada Council
people did in the hauling of the boats up the Volga. In our own country we likewise have a culture of our own. It certainly is just beginning to grow, but we are a new country and we must recognize that fact. Yet we have a song in Canada that is known from one end of the country to the other and is sung in the minds and hearts of everybody.

An hon. member across the way says "Alouette". Certainly it is "Alouette". You hear it sung on the farms and in the homes of British Columbia just as you hear it sung in Quebec and Ontario. There we find the beginning of culture. It is something that cannot be taken from us. The reason the Hungarians revolted was that their culture grew from within them. They had the singing hearts, the singing minds, with the freedom they have always felt in their music, in their songs and in their dancing; and they were not prepared to give it up. But when you have a central organization begin to tell you that we in Canada should foster the ballet or we should foster another form of culture, that is wrong in itself.
It is the demand of the people who go to these things that will determine exactly what the people want to see.
Now, to suggest that people are against culture is to suggest that no one enjoys the theatre; that no one enjoys the music that is all about us, that no one enjoys the songs and dances that we have seen so often performed by the Ukranians and other ethnic groups in this country. How false can we get? These are things we must remember in connection with our thoughts respecting the Canada Council.
Yesterday the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke raised several questions in my mind when he spoke. I should like the Prime Minister when he replies to define what he had in mind when he used the terms, "spiritual development and intellectual world brotherhood". I should like him to elaborate on that and explain to us how those two terms are going to be embodied within the terms of this bill. I ask him, too, if he would tell us about the change in the decision that was made in respect to the remuneration that is going to be paid to the executives who administer the council.
Arising out of this, sir, is one important factor, because culture will develop no matter whether or not we set up this organization. That factor is education, which comes within the scope of culture itself. If we do not have education we have no culture, at least of the finer type.

If you will just listen, sonny, you will learn something. On page 15 he says:
The attitudes and the ideas of the boys and girls are likely to reflect in a true and real sense the attitudes and the values of their parents and of the peoples in the communities in which the boys and girls are brought up. For me, it is nonsense to expect teachers and schools to do for young people things that are not being carried out by parents and citizens around them.
Therein lies your culture, within the local district, sir. It is nonsense, he says, to expect the teachers and schools to do for the young people things that are not being carried out by the parents and citizens around them.
When I read that some of my friends and colleagues get up and damn and blast the teachers of the high schools because the youngsters do not work hard enough or do not acquire sufficient knowledge of this or that or the other, X feel that that, if true, is the responsibility that has to be shared by all of us, and its major burden must rest, not on the teachers and the schools or the department of education, but upon the nature of society and the standards of values that we develop in it, and the goals and objectives that we ourselves hold for ourselves and for our young people and, if our ideal is to get more for less, that is, to work shorter hours and get more pay-and X am not objecting to that-that may be a proper goal- then you cannot expect institutions not to be affected by that attitude and that point of view.
Sir, the point he makes, in effect, is that here we have a society in which we are blaming the teachers, the educationists; but they are not necessarily at fault because the influence of the home, the church and the whole society about us is reflected in the attitude, actions and culture of the boys and girls within our own country. We are building up a "gimme" attitude in this country, and it is wrong. I would suggest, sir, that instead we should remember that as you sow so shall you reap, and that would be a much better form of culture to promote in this country.
Then on the following page, page 16, he explains the need for sacrifice. This is an educationist of the finest type speaking:
[Mr. Hahn.l
Education ... is almost the most important; more important than highways, bridges, ferries or pipe lines, on which we spend so much money.
Now, sir, we agree with him wholeheartedly in every possible way. Here we have the very embodiment of everything cultural for which the people of this country should stand, and we have it being put aside for a promotional scheme of another type, unless I misinterpreted the Prime Minister when he said that none of these funds will be made available to the sciences.
Then, sir, I ask you, who would make these sacrifices? It would be the old age pensioners, the blind, the needy of this country, who contribute through indirect taxes just as much as anyone else does to the setting up of this particular fund. These are the people who are least able to afford it. I continue quoting from the middle of page 16, where he goes on to speak about the fact that the intelligence of the pupils today is no different from what it was at other times. But then on page 17 he has this to say:
I have for years urged the establishment of a general scheme of scholarships, bursaries and interest-free loans for all able and industrious young men and women . . .
We would agree with that; we would agree with the need for those things. There is every need in the world; but I would say that possibly the most important statement is made on page 18, when he demonstrates to these people the problem which exists today:
I think we should try to achieve in our schools, and our university for that matter, as great a challenge to every individual-an intellectual challenge-that we possibly can, and as great a variety, because of the natural differences between human beings.
Now we are proposing to bring culture through the Canada Council, which will decide what is best for us in the way of a cultural environment and that, in itself, is wrong because it does not develop the individual.
He carries on and says:
And so I would suggest, if moneys are available, and I think they can be made available, that we use them at the school level in strengthening the staffs, if that is possible, in terms of finding teachers, adding to their numbers, adding to their qualifications and training, adding, if necessary to achieve those things, to their salaries, adding to their prestige, to the importance that we associate with them and attach to them in the community.
It was my privilege during the summer to discuss this problem of teacher training and the shortage of teachers with one of my friends, a university professor. I found that he had just such a problem within his own faculty. I found that he had to have an instructor in the field of science. Finally he found one man who had published upwards of

30 papers, was the author of a book and had excellent qualifications. I have learned since that this man has proven to be an excellent instructor. The university could only offer him $5,200 a year. Here was a man who had experience, who, it is true, came from another land. He wanted to get out of that foreign land, and he decided that he would take that salary because he wanted the job; he wanted to live in Canada.
What does industry offer in comparison? It offers $7,000 and $8,000 to a non-qualified individual, just a raw recruit, with his PhD. Sir, here we have another instance. We might compare it with the people to the south of us, where I understand the average earnings are something like $10,500 for nine months, and those earnings can be supplemented by summer work to bring them up to some $14,000.

My hon. friends say we must allow the people to develop their own culture. Well, of course, one does not have to talk about that sort of thing; it is a well-known fact. There is only one way in which culture can be developed, and that is through the efforts of the individuals themselves.
As I read the clauses of this bill, and particularly one of the clauses, one of the objects of the institution which is envisaged is to help those people in their efforts to promote culture. What this culture is to be is not to be dictated from the top. However, I am not prepared to wait two or three thousand years or for all eternity in

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to encourage the arts, humanities and social sciences in Canada. I do not think anyone can disagree, and certainly I do not, with the fundamental purpose of the measure as thus set out. It is laudable and represents something for which we on this side of the house have been pressing for some time. As far as I am concerned personally I am delighted to see that action is finally being taken in this regard.
But having said that, Mr. Speaker, I think it is necessary to examine for a few moments one or two of the ways in which this avowed purpose is going to be accomplished, and having examined these methods I think it would be in order to suggest that perhaps they are not the best possible means by which to accomplish the stated objectives.
As I understand it, the bill essentially comprises in one piece of legislation two undertakings which are quite different in nature. The first is the provision of a substantial capital sum of $50 million to be distributed among Canadian universities as construction grants, this distribution to take place over a period of time which is not specified in the bill but which it has been suggested by the minister would be about 10 years. The other purpose is the support of cultural activities in this country indefinitely into the future by means of the interest on a fund also of $50 million to be contributed by the government at the inception of the plan. The only reason for linking these two dissimilar propositions in one bill is that in each case the money is to be administered by the same body, the Canada Council.
Speaking first and briefly with regard to the question of grants for university construction, while one may question to some extent the wisdom of supplying this money as
128$

Canada Council
a lump sum rather than in amounts as required year by year for the purpose, there may be at least a substantial argument in favour of the lump sum proposition. The construction of major buildings and extensive additional facilities for universities is not something that can be carried on in such a way as to use exactly the same amount of funds each year. It may very well be that in the initial stages as the plan gets under way only small sums will be required; then subsequently over a period of years as the plans come into being substantial sums will be required as the universities hasten to get the much-needed buildings constructed and into operation.
A good deal of leeway must be given to anyone who is going to have the disposition of these funds, and for that reason I am not inclined to quarrel too much with it, though I would have been happier had we been giving this money by means of parliamentary grants. As I say, I am not going to quarrel too much with the way it has been done.
Turning now to the grants for cultural activities, the remaining $50 million, it is quite apparent that the same type of argument which I have set forth in relation to the construction grants does not apply in this second case. These grants consist of numerous contributions of small amounts for manifold purposes to a multitude of individuals and organizations across this country. According to the Prime Minister the sum total of these contributions is expected to be in the neighbourhood of $2 million or perhaps somewhat less per year. It is expected that they will continue at that rate indefinitely into the future. For that purpose there is to be given to this Canada Council a sum of $50 million with complete freedom as to the way in which they shall invest it, with no restraining influences being placed upon the nature of the market operations they may undertake. The purpose of the endowment will be to produce that $2 million per year.
I suggest that when annual incomes are concerned and when annual expenditures are to be made by a creature of this federal government, because that is the purpose of the Canada Council; when comparatively equal expenditures are to be made on a continuing basis, they should be voted by parliamentary appropriations so that parliament may be in position to scrutinize and examine the way in which the taxpayers' money is being used. Make no mistake about it, and I shall return to this point later, the money which is going to this Canada Council is the taxpayers' money just as much as any other dollar which is spent by the government of Canada.

It was suggested by the Prime Minister in his earlier remarks that he wanted to remove the operation of these cultural grants from the influence of parliament. Listening to the Prime Minister one would have almost thought there was something wicked about this House of Commons, that we as a body were not to be trusted with any measure of control or supervision over the operation of these cultural grants. I do not know why. We represent the country as a whole and some of us perhaps have a wider experience in cultural matters than others, but I think all of us have sympathy with them. I cannot quite understand why the Prime Minister should have taken the attitude that we are unqualified to deal with it or, worse still, that we would engage in machinations and devious methods to defeat the purposes of this Canada Council. As I see it, that is the only argument he can put forth as to why he wants to take it away from us. If there is no reason why it should be taken away, surely it is proper that parliament should continue to scrutinize these expenditures.
Mark this, the setting up of this amount as an endowment fund and its transfer to the Canada Council does not remove the fund from parliamentary control. Parliament is supreme, and it can change the terms and conditions of this legislation at any time. Parliament can, if it wishes take the fund back into its own possession. The Canada Council is a creature of this parliament and is subject at all times, by legislation, to the control of this parliament. But what the measure does do, and this is important, is to remove its operations in large measure from the detailed scrutiny of this body.
There is a great deal of difference. If such dangers exist as the Prime Minister set forth, and I do not admit that they do, it does not matter whether or not the fund is established as an endowment fund, because of the preeminent position of parliament in respect to all such legislation. The only thing this endowment fund does in respect to these cultural activities is to remove them from the annual scrutiny of parliament as an item in the estimates of this body. I suggest that is a serious matter.
However, to my mind what is most wrong about the government's attitude and explanation in introducing this legislation was the Prime Minister's departure into a new field of public finance. Over the last number of years we have become accustomed to something called cyclical budgeting, but I suggest that not until this year have we heard of windfall budgeting. This is an interesting new departure, a departure by which the government with a particularly needed project in mind sits on its hands and waits

one year, two years, three years, tour years, and then in the fifth year, according to this windfall theory of budgeting, it suddenly has a substantial additional revenue with which it can carry on this particular project.
You cannot operate a federal government on that basis with any measure of continuing success. Mr. Speaker, we cannot expect to budget amounts totalling in excess of $5,000 million in the same way one would operate a peanut stand, rushing out to get a new mirror to hang behind the counter should someone come in and purchase an excessive amount of candy on a particular day. The government has to accept the responsibility for undertaking projects when those projects become necessary, and the Prime Minister has admitted that this has been necessary for a number of years. You cannot wait until someone dies in order to carry a plan forward.
As it was explained to us, the Prime Minister did not say this was a major factor in the establishment of this endowment fund but he told us-breaking, incidentally, the regulations of the Dominion Succession Duty Act regarding secrecy in so doing-that two big estates had become subject to succession duties in the past year, and that was a major factor in deciding on this endowment. As I have said, Mr. Speaker, that is totally, absolutely and completely wrong, because it tries to hide the fact that it is the taxpayers, all of them taken together, who are contributing to the financing of this council. However tortuous the path which the Prime Minister may attempt to follow, this is not a project of two great Canadian industrialists who by fortuitous circumstances passed away in the same year, leaving the government with a substantial sum of money.
We have in this country something called the consolidated revenue fund, and the money from these estates is paid into that fund in exactly the same way it is paid in from the estates of the smallest taxpayers, in exactly the same way it is paid in by all of us who contribute during our lifetime in the form of income tax. That consolidated revenue fund, as the Prime Minister himself stated in another section of his remarks, is the fund from which this money will be paid. It has no connection with the estates of the two gentlemen who have been referred to. They were both, in their lifetimes, fine Canadian citizens. They prospered in this country and contributed greatly to this country, and it may even have been, that they would have liked to see this particular path followed in the use of their money.
But by what right does the Prime Minister assume that credit for this project is to be
Canada Council
attributed to two individuals, no matter how worthy, and taken away from the thousands upon thousands of taxpayers in this country who have contributed their mites to this proposal? I think, and I am sorry to have to say this, that the explanation to which I have just referred-the "windfall budget" explanation-is nothing more than a piece of cynical opportunism, and I regret deeply that the Prime Minister should have felt it necessary to follow the particular path he did.
Sir, it may very well have been in his mind that he wanted to do two things. First of all, in this year of government plenty he may have felt that an anticipated surplus of some $300 million or $500 million was embarrassing. It may well have been that the government was desirous of distributing- "hiding" would be the better word-as much of that surplus as possible before the end of the fiscal year in order that the taxpayers of this country might not have clearly set out for them the extent of overtaxation by the present government.
Again, Mr. Speaker, it may very well have been that this was chosen as a means of glossing over the fact that this procedure by way of endowment fund is not the proper way in which a continuing parliamentary expenditure should be undertaken, a method of diverting attention from the fact that a $50 million slice was being taken for cultural activities when, actually, a contribution of $2 million, statutory in nature, over the next number of years indefinitely into the future would have accomplished exactly the same purpose. But of course, as I pointed out, that brings us full circle to the unfortunate fact for the government that if the road of proper parliamentary control had been followed, this $50 million for the endowment of cultural activities could not have been extracted from the consolidated revenue fund for this year, and the government surplus would therefore be some $50 million higher.
I realize, of course, that this argument is unattractive to the Prime Minister. When it was advanced by my leader on February 5 the Prime Minister interrupted him to say:
On reflection I do not think the hon. gentleman will consider that his first remark that this was probably done because the government felt it was going to be embarrassed with a surplus and had to truck it away somewhere was fair. I do not think it is worthy of the discussion on this Canada Council.
That was his opinion then, and I daresay it continues to be his opinion. I have considered the matter carefully, and as far as I am concerned I think it is a very worthy subject for discussion at this time. I think anything which concerns the expenditure of

Canada Council
$100 million of the taxpayers' money and the possible reasons for it is a very apt subject for discussion in this house.
Of course few men can carry off an emotional argument as well as the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker. He is dignified. He is fresh and young looking, and when his lips pout a little emotion rises and it is hard not to get a lump in one's throat and feel a mist of tears across the eyes. And when we say things about him one is tempted to consider how Caesar must have felt when Brutus stabbed him. Well, Caesars quite often get shocking surprises, though not many of them have the good fortune which the Prime Minister has had to be their own Mark Antony afterwards. I placed very little credence in his observations anent this matter the first time it was brought up for consideration.
I want to summarize in this way, Mr. Speaker. The purpose of this legislation is good. I voted for it at the resolution stage. I will vote for it as a bill. I am glad that finally, after five long years' delay, it has been brought before this house. I have no argument with the essential purpose; but I contend that in the case of the endowment fund for cultural activity the method of financing which is being proposed is an unsatisfactory one from the view point of established parliamentary procedure and parliamentary control, and that the purpose behind this course of action has been to sterilize as large a portion as possible of this year's surplus so the taxpayers of this country may be misled.

Mr. Speaker, I consider that there is now before the house a measure the benefits of which to Canadian generations to come will outlive those of any piece of legislation I know of since confederation. I feel that the measure establishes for future Canadians the possibility of enlightenment.
I was provoked to rise by the hon. member for New Westminster, when he almost challengingly suggested that there were no members on the Liberal side of the house who

spoke on the measure. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that we consider this measure to be of a class of which, comparatively speaking, it can be said, to quote Shakespeare, that we do not have to gild the lily. But I was rather surprised to find that there were any members in the house who oppose the legislation.
Each of us in his own way and according to his own capacity attempts to assess a piece of legislation. When we find arguments which are contrary to those which we believe, we like to assess them according to our ability.
I have been waiting to hear from the Social Credit speakers who have been opposing this measure a tangible, logical argument so I may be able to assess it. The only thing they have said is that, in their opinion, there are enough existing organizations to disseminate culture, and they refer to the provincial organizations.
I ask you this question, Mr. Speaker. Could there ever be enough institutions to disseminate culture and education? I do not think any such institution in the country should be able to take the position that we already have sufficient education, that we already have sufficient culture, and that there is no room for any more such institutions.
That is a pitiful fallacy, unless there is some fear that education should become more widespread. I do not suggest that the Social Credit party have any fear lest people become more educated, nor that they have any fear that light or education may make it possible for people to understand their preachings, their teachings or their philosophies. But I should like for a moment to make reference to a quotation which might be somewhat informative. I am quoting very briefly from G. W. Curtis, a philosopher who had this to say:
The sure foundations of the state are laid in knowledge, not in ignorance; and every interference with education, culture, booklearning, which is the recorded wisdom of the experience of mankind is the demagogue's sneer at intelligent liberty, inviting national degeneracy and ruin.
I feel that if arguments were presented that could show a fault with regard to educating, with regard to spreading culture, with regard to spreading appreciation of the arts and music, then of course we might be able to judge from their arguments. But when they attempt to interfere with it-and I say without hesitation that I interpret their opposition to this bill as a direct attempt to interfere with the spreading of knowledge and culture in this country; and perhaps I do them an injustice and interpret it wrongly- I wonder whether they have ever heard of or read the words of a man named Everett, who said:	,111111

Education is a better safeguard of liberty than a standing army. If we retrench the wages of the schoolmaster, we must raise those of the recruiting sergeant.
When you hear an expression such as, for example, that which we heard from the hon. member for New Westminster to the effect that the museum in Ottawa is of no particular value in Canada, what are you to think? I must say that I was astonished at the statement. By the widest stretch of my imagination, and as charitable as I should like to be in interpreting that statement, I could not find the least basis for its justification. I had hoped that this measure, because of its very character and its very nature, would have the support of the entire house without any qualification and without any limitations.
I was strongly impressed by the remarks made by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) when he briefly highlighted the value of this measure. I believe that in the generations to come-and I speak for myself at this moment, Mr. Speaker-I will feel proud to know that I had the privilege and honour of being a member of this house when a measure of this kind was debated for the future of Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of speaking in this debate, but I am prompted to do so after listening to the speeches that have been made by the hon. member for Saskatoon and the hon. member for Cartier. They have made statements that are wild and fantastically false. It would appear from what both of them have said that to have conformity is the be-all and end-all of culture. As I listened to both of them I realized how aptly a particular quotation from a book by Wilfred Trotter, F.R.S., "Art and Science in Medicine," Oxford University Press, 1941, would apply. This is a brief quotation:
Whether or not it is true that the age of adventure in the physical world is now closed, adventure in the world of thought is still open to every soul that is not wholly tamed and in love with the cage. It has always been more difficult than adventure in the ordinary sense, and it is becoming more difficult every day. Uniformity of thought is increasingly the apparent goal and demand of civilization; education has no use for the fires of rebellion, and even science itself is not above lending an occasional hand at the fire engine. Still, there burns on in most of us a small wild spark. I advise you to cherish it as a precious possession. Do not, however, be under any misapprehension. Really to think for oneself is as strange, difficult, and dangerous as any adventure, and, as the wise ones say, "it will do you no good"; but, like virtue-which it does not otherwise greatly resemble-it will be its own reward.
I mentioned at the outset I had no intention of taking part in this debate, but now I do intend to say a few words. I shall make my remarks brief because I appreciate that 82715-82
Canada Council
the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is anxious to answer some of the questions that have been raised during this discussion. I am sure that during the course of the debate all of us have learned something on the subject of culture. For one thing, we have learned that it is difficult to define, and in my opinion it is a subject upon which it is dangerously misleading to generalize. I think that this, in itself, ought to make us realize how important it is to give most careful and thoughtful consideration as to the best methods of promoting culture in our country. I believe that is the crux of our problem and the only area of difference between Social Crediters and other members who are supporting this bill.
The very fact that we have heard various interpretations of culture and the best way of promoting it in Canada seems to point out that it involves individualistic concepts, and that the concept of regimentation or creating a mass cultural formula is absolutely false. In my humble opinion we ought to set out in clear, definite terms in the charter setting up the Canada Council that the council will avoid any restrictions or interference with the creative independence or intellectual freedom of an individual. If the council in any way promotes conformity, as is apparently the argument advanced by the hon. member who just resumed his seat, then I believe that the Canada Council will do irreparable harm to cultural efforts in our country. I wish to remind hon. members of the house of recent history which indicates precisely the sort of thing to which I am referring. In a publication issued by the press and information office of the German federal government, there appears the following under the chapter devoted to cultural policy:
The national socialist state set up with incomparable ruthlessness a cultural regime and monopoly organized in separate reich culture chambers along strictly totalitarian and propagandistic lines. These led to complete lack of freedom in all branches of art and culture and paralyzed the entire cultural life of the nation.
We have learned other things as well in this discussion. One of the things we have learned is that the government of Canada has done very little to encourage the appreciation of the arts themselves or given encouragement to the great talents that exist in our country. Now, apart from the encouragement of the arts and encouragement of an appreciative public, there is of course the prime consideration of the function of culture and the humanities in any nation. We know that in addition to the great French and English cultures which form the very basis of our national life, there are within our borders millions of people of diverse ethnic origins who are enriching the cultural fabric

Canada Council
of our nation. We note that each of these has been welcomed into Canada and they owe a new political allegiance to our country which they must accept. But we wish to emphasize that the Canada Council must make it perfectly clear that it recognizes the value of diversity, and that there is quality and purpose in preserving the cultural heritage of all these people. I am confident that together our people will weave a truly dynamic and distinctly Canadian type of culture.
As stated by Professor Watson Kirkconnell in his introduction to some new Canadian verse, "Canadian Overtones Winnipeg", Columbia Press, 1935, in relation to our situation in Canada, "If we accept Wilhelm von Humboldt's absolute and essential value of human development in its diversity, then we shall take every opportunity of saving for our country each valuable element of individuality which we can obtain."
Now, Mr. Speaker, this event to set up the Canada Council, in a sense, does make a page in the history of our parliament. We all recognize the need of encouraging the arts and introducing gracious living into Canada. Indeed, such an effort is worthy of the support, not only of the members of this house but of every Canadian who realizes the importance of lifting our thinking beyond the purely materialistic concepts that crowd our everyday life.
Since I have said that, it is obvious that we in the Social Credit party are for and not against the ultimate objective of stimulating cultural activities. Where we differ from the Liberal party and the C.C.F. party is in the method by which this desirable objective should be realized. The present administration proposes to set up the council and endow it with a $100 million fund, and away it is supposed to go with a never-to-be questioned attitude as to how the cultural achievement is to be made.
We would like to know to whom the council should be responsible? Surely, if public money is to be used it is important for us to know that the council will never become what some newspapers have said it could become, namely a political pork barrel disguised under the cloak of culture. We would also like to know who will constitute the membership of this council. Why should the government deny us this information? In what way will such information impair the formation of the council?
We would like to know why the government does not make these funds available to the respective provincial governments and earmark them for the express purpose of cultural activities in the respective provinces.

In the province of Alberta, for example, we have had a cultural development branch associated with the department of economic affairs for many long years, and it is doing an excellent job. Within that department there is a general department of cultural activities. It services the cultural activities and administrative details of cultural activity boards within our province: drama, music, handicrafts and visual arts, recreation and libraries. These are all dealt with by the cultural activities branch of the department. This department encourages and stimulates an interest in each of these activities by providing organizational, teaching and financial assistance.
We have the drama section which assists communities in organizing dramatic productions, and conducts workshops and advises on other aspects of theatre. There is a music section which assists in organizing communities in various phases of music activities: festivals, productions, bands, orchestras and choral groups. We have a handicrafts and visual arts section, which assists in organization of provincial craft centres. Teachers are provided in design of leather, copper, woodwork, ceramics and weaving. No charges are made to the public.
We have a recreation section which assists communities in the province to establish recreational centres and programs which cover all phases of recreational activity. A leadership school is conducted at Red Deer each summer. Similar centres in our province provide clinics during certain seasons and assist in establishing leaders in various fields of sport activity.
We have a library section which administers the public libraries act and assist in encouraging the establishment and development of library facilities. The government also assists libraries financially. Various scholarships are offered to deserving talent within our province.
We would like to know why some of these funds are not made available to that level of government which is closest to the people. I for one should like to see a limit on the number of national agencies in this field because I do believe there is always a danger of duplication, and eventually the work is at cross purposes. Furthermore, we in the Social Credit group believe that federally directed lessons in culture are not the answer to this problem; in fact, the very reverse is true.
In his opening address on this matter the Prime Minister mentioned the various countries that have similar boards as an indication that perhaps we should follow the same plan. I was particularly interested in what he said with respect to the West German

Republic. I am quite familiar with the conditions in that country and I wish to assure the Prime Minister that the cultural effort in the West German Republic is on a decentralized basis and is the result of co-ordination and rationalization between the federal and the provincial governments, so to speak. I quote from the same book to which I referred a few moments ago:
Since 1949 the ministers of culture of the Laender are co-ordinated on a federal level by the permanent conference of cultural ministers. Where super-regional affairs are involved effecting several or all Laender, this conference is resolved, out of state-political and cultural historical motives, to see that its cultural-political work suffers no infringements by the Bund. Constitutionally, the ministers have at their disposal a federal organ in the cultural committee of the Bundesrat, through which they are able to voice and make felt their standpoint regarding federal cultural questions.
Farther on this quotation appears:
The goal is, to find a solution of the question of furthering super-regional art and cultural problems through co-ordination and rationalization between the Laender and the Bund which, while clearly defining the areas of interest of each, at the same time guarantee mutual and uniform cultural endeavours similar to those which have developed between the Laender and the communes. Hence the furtherance of scientific research is a task which must be carried out mutually by the Bund and the Laender. But despite the prevailing interest of the democratic state for such institutions, restriction of their independency and supervision of their intellectual freedom by the government must be avoided.
In concluding my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I repeat, we believe the question of furthering our national cultural effort in Canada at this time can be best resolved through such coordination between the federal and the provincial governments, for the simple reason that the federal government cannot in any way, nor can the Canada Council, know the peculiar circumstances which prevail in the various communities of Canada. The cooperation of the provincial governments in this respect is an essential factor for that very reason.

In the course of the discussion thus far, very little has been said about providing scholarships from the endowment fund. The emphasis has been on assistance in the furtherance of culture. I am not quarrelling for one minute, Mr. Chairman, with the idea of payments being made to promote culture in Canada; I think that is a very worthy objective. But, as I understand the bill, there is also the power to use the proceeds of this fund for the granting of scholarships, both undergraduate and post-graduate, to Canadians and to scholars coming here from abroad.
The universities therefore come into the picture in two ways. First by assistance for their building projects from the $50 million fund and then they come into it by way of scholarships to needy students. I would hope that is not to be a minor part of the use made of the endowment fund.
The assistance to the universities is particularly important, of course, to all of us who are interested in Canadian universities from coast to coast. As to the university of British Columbia, those of us who are getting on in years were compelled to go to an eastern university in order to get a degree. Our university of British Columbia has been established for only about 40 years. Hence in that province we are now seeing the full benefit from a university. I can remember the day when there were few university graduates in the whole province. We now have graduates

Canada Council
of our own university in every centre in the province and giving splendid leadership in every field.
The chancellor of the University of British Columbia is the Honourable Chief Justice Sherwood Lett who was one of the graduates in the early days. Under his leadership and under the leadership of Dr. Norman A. M. MacKenzie as president wonderful things are being done by that university in spite of great difficulties. They have the second largest enrolment in Canada and are greatly handicapped by lack of buildings. They have students coming there from all over the world. I think they are contributing not only to our province but to the whole of the nation and, in fact, in a much wider field. This measure of assistance that will be provided by this bill is therefore of the utmost importance to the University of British Columbia and to the people of that province.
I am sorry that opposition has been expressed in just the way it has been done in the course of this debate. However, I think the Prime Minister will agree with me that parliament must be kept in the closest touch with this whole project. That provision is necessary, of course, in respect of every body that is set up by parliament. It is a sound principle that parliament must have the opportunity to check most carefully what is done by all of these governmental bodies. That principle applies particularly with regard to the Canada Council because it will depend for its success not only on the personnel, the men and women who are appointed, but also on a thorough understanding of its work by the Canadian people and the deepest sort of sympathy with that work.
1 do not know how such objectives can be achieved if provision is not made for discussion in parliament of the work of the council. If we simply set aside $100 million, then the government appoints the members of the council and they proceed with their work, the general public-the people of Canada as a whole-will be quite unable to follow what is being done. Antagonisms may be built up. There may be criticisms of the work of the council which cannot be met. The proper way in which to remedy that situation is to make certain that parliament reviews the work of the council every year.
If the bill goes through in its present form, there will be no item in the estimates for the Canada Council unless the government should see fit to bring in a vote annually. I suppose we could question the minister who is responsible for the Council when the first item of his estimates is under discussion. However, that is an unsatisfactory way in which to deal with the situation. Many other
[Mr. Green.l
items under that minister's supervision will be discussed on the first item and we could not have a proper debate on the work of the Canada Council. One way of bringing about a satisfactory result would be to show in the estimates a vote for the Canada Council just in the same way that we show a vote for atomic energy or for the national research council. They are both listed as separate votes, as the Prime Minister knows. They are not listed under any particular minister. They appear as separate votes and they have to be dealt with as such. Hence there can be, for example, a full discussion on the work of the national research council when the estimates for that council are called.
If an amendment of the type I have mentioned is made to the bill, I think we can be certain that every year there will be a debate on the work of the Canada Council. The danger is not next year perhaps or the year after that; but as time goes on, it will become all the more important that there has been some method of keeping parliament closely in contact with what is being done by this new council. I therefore hope that the Prime Minister will see that the bill is amended to meet this particular situation.

speechtext:
Clause 2 is an interpretative clause defining the term "the arts". I do not think we have any objection to the interpretation given here, but the purpose of the bill is to encourage the arts, humanities and social sciences. I am wondering why no interpretation is given to th!e other two branches, the humanities and social sciences. So far as I can see, there is more need for an interpretation of the humanities and social sciences than there is any need for an interpretation of what is meant by the arts. I think almost everyone would agree that we know what "the arts" means.
While I am speaking on that, may I remind you, Mr. Chairman, that the other day when we were in committee I had something to say about the social sciences. I think we need to interpret that a little
Canada Council
bit because the term "social sciences" can take in a lot of territory, so much territory that perhaps the council will be embarking on some form of work which is in reality none of its business. I know something about the social science textbooks that are used in some of our schools. I have not been a father trying to care for my children's education without reading some of the social science books which come to my home. I must say that I am not enamoured of some of the things that are taught in social science.
When we were in committee a few days ago I read a paragraph from a book which I have, entitled "Education or Indoctrination", in which something is said with respect to the social science textbook. The paragraph reads:
In 1940 Dr. Raply Robey made an examination of 600 social science textbooks in high schools. He declared, "A substantial portion of the social science textbooks now used in high schools tend to criticize our form of government, and hold in derision or contempt the system of private enterprise . . . There is a notable tendency in the books to play down what has been accomplished in this country and to stress the defects of our democracy."
It is that sort of thing to which I object. However, in this clause we are discussing the interpretation of the arts. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I think if the council were only concerned with the arts as described in clause 2, we would not have had as much to say as we had. I do not think the attitude that this group took would have been the same. It is to some of the other things that are not interpreted in this clause that we have taken objection in our speeches.
May I ask the Prime Minister why it is that the other two branches of the work of this council, the humanities and social sciences, are not given an interpretation in this bill as the expression "the arts" has been?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
It was considered that the term "the arts" should be defined so as not to extend it beyond those arts that it was intended should be fostered by the Canada Council. The other expressions, the humanities and social sciences, have a recognized and accepted meaning in the academic world. I notice that in the academic world the term humanities includes such studies as history, literature, foreign languages, philosophy and related subjects; that is the generally accepted meaning that is given to this term in the universities. I think the term "social sciences" is generally taken to mean the study of anthropology, economics, geography, law-not municipal law, but law in its

Canada Council
general, broad application-political science, psychology, sociology and the related subjects.
I would not think that the Canada Council would have any jurisdiction whatever to determine the textbooks that would be used in high schools in connection with the study of the social sciences; that is something that would be outside of their jurisdiction. The purpose would be for the council to encourage the study and development of the arts, humanities and social sciences in their broad aspects, as they affect the enjoyment of life in an organized, civilized society. It was not considered that it would be necessary to describe the humanities or the social sciences, but it was felt that the arts should be defined in a way that would include those things that we in our generation recognize to be the arts. The definition includes the arts of the theatre. Well, the arts of the theatre are the drama, the opera, even the ballet, those things that are provided for the enjoyment of the audiences that attend the theatre; architecture, the arts of the theatre, literature, music, painting, sculpture, the graphic arts, and other similar creative and interpretative activities are mentioned.
There was no attempt made to restrict the objectives, but as the phrase "the arts" is used in describing the objects of the Canada Council, it was felt there should be an indication there that it covered quite a wide field of these interpretative and creative activities that do give so much enjoyment to people generally.

speechtext: My simple point is this. To my way of thinking the term "the arts" is in much less need of interpretation than are the humanities and social services which have not been interpreted.

Mr. Chairman, there are many people in the country, of course, who look on the establishment of the Canada Council as one more step in the centralization of power and administration in the federal government. There are many people who are concerned lest it become another instrument for intruding a federal hand into provincial affairs. While we were considering section 3 it occurred to us that some amendment could be made which would perhaps go some distance toward allaying the fears of many people in that regard.
In answer to a question a moment ago I heard the Prime Minister say that it would be the intention of the governor in council to appoint a representative to the council from each province. I think that would be quite proper but I believe it would be better if the governor in council could select nine appointees and allow the provincial governments to name a representative to the council from their province. This would permit them to feel they had some representation on the council that would see to it that full consideration was given to the desires of the province. In my judgment it would be a great protection and comfort to the Prime Minister if he were to have the provinces tied into the council as partners. For that reason I move the following amendment:
That all the words after the word "members" in the fifth line be deleted and the following words substituted:
"Nine of which shall be appointed by the governor in council and one to be appointed by each of the provincial governments".
I would urge that the Prime Minister give very careful consideration to that amendment which I think would clear away many of his problems.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am afraid the ultimate result would be just the opposite of what the hon. gentleman has in mind. I feel that what we are endeavouring to do, namely set up a body that would not be subject to partisan political consideration would not be assisted at all by having one appointee to represent each of the ten provincial governments. I believe we

should choose an appointee from each province, not as representing the province but rather as being a qualified person residing in each of the ten provinces. Such an appointee would be apt to have more intimate knowledge of the conditions in the province in which he resided than would others who might reside elsewhere. I would imagine that my friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra would have a more intimate knowledge of what was the situation in regard to the activities in which this council would be engaged in British Columbia than would someone who resided in Prince Edward Island or in Newfoundland. I think a qualified person residing in each of the provinces should be chosen but I do not think they should be on the council to act, as it were, as the mouthpiece of the provincial government. I do not think this would make for the kind of operation that would be generally regarded in any part of the country as being above party politics.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
I listened carefully and I think sympathetically to what the Prime Minister had to say in opposition to the motion I have made. I hope no words of mine conveyed the idea that I thought that each of these members of the council who would be appointed by provincial governments would be looked upon as being a representative of a provincial government. Can the Prime Minister maintain that position in the light of the fact that the government is going to appoint nineteen? Are we to assume that, when the government of Canada appoints nineteen, those appointees will be representatives of the federal government? Not at all, and I am not interpreting it that way.
I believe that each provincial government is just as likely to choose a representative of the people of that province as the Prime Minister and his government would be likely to choose nineteen people. I shall go further. We do not suggest by any means that they be mouthpieces of the governments. We want them to be truly representative of the people of the province. I think they are more likely to represent the people of the province and the will of the people if they are selected by a body which represents the province in the government of this country.
I have every faith in every one of the provincial governments and in their ability to select someone who is fully qualified. I feel sure he would be a representative of the people of a province and not a mouthpiece of the government. Certainly he would be in a far better position to judge whether the things done by the Canada Council were in the interests of the people. If you have nine of them appointed by some body other than

the governor in council you will have at least a fair-sized body of opinion on the Canada Council which would be watching more carefully to see that things are done in the interests of the people themselves and not of the government that appoints the whole council.
That is my position and I feel that the Prime Minister's objections cannot be maintained as valid arguments.

There are people who consider themselves to be the intelligentsia, people who work together world-wide with their friends toward a certain goal. They have been at it for many generations. These people could gain absolute control of this council just by putting the right kind of pressure on certain places in Ottawa. There would be no way in which the provinces could modify or influence that trend.
What the hon. member for Peace River has proposed is one little safeguard. There is no use our discussing UNESCO and then before we get to UNESCO tying the hands of the governments so they cannot do the things that ought to be done or use the kind of safeguard this amendment provides against perversion and subversion.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is another point about this amendment I should like to bring out. I stand ready to be corrected, but I believe most provincial governments have a department or branch dealing with cultural matters. The provincial governments and the people of the provinces are just as interested in the cultural arts and humanities and social sciences as is this government. I cannot think that they would be less favourable to the appointment of someone who had no political affiliation than would this government. I do not think that a provincial government would necessarily go out and appoint someone of its particular political stripe. I think they would appoint

Canada Council
someone who they thought was most able and most adapted to the appointment.
There is one thing. The government here is going to appoint nine members, even if this amendment should carry, plus an additional three appointments, or a total of twelve appointments. Surely, out of 22 appointments the sovereign government of a province should have the right to make one? One in 23 is not asking too much.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is making a mistake, I am sure it is involuntary. The number is 21 over all-19, plus the chairman and vice-chairman. It is not 22 or 23. It is 21.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Yes, it is 21, including the director.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: The director is not a member of the council.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Well, he will have a lot to do with it just the same. They meet several times a year. They do not do the actual work; the council does the actual work. I think it will be something like the board of governors of the C.B.C. The management carries on the actual work, but the board of governors meets occasionally to give advice, look over financial statements and listen to grievances. I imagine something similar will happen in the case of the Canada Council. All I am saying is that to ask that the provincial governments should each have the right to appoint one to a council with a directorate of 21 is not asking too much.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, rightly or
wrongly, this Canada Council is being set up by the dominion government, and that government is accepting full responsibility; and in view of that fact I doubt very much the wisdom of turning round and saying that the provinces must appoint a certain number of members to the council. I suggest that the government here must be kept responsible for the work of the council. No doubt, the provincial governments are all interested, but it is not their responsibility. They are not being asked to accept any responsibility under this bill; why should they be asked to become half responsible by appointing one member each to the council?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: So that we won't all be fugitives from the brain gang.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that it would not be very efficient organization to set up a council of that type, with the dominion appointing a certain number of members and each of ten provinces appointing one. After all, this is not a dominion-federal

project; it is a dominion project, and I think that if only for the benefit of those who may wish to criticize this council, and criticize it very seriously in the years that lie ahead, it would be far wiser to keep it as a dominion council; and then any mistakes that are going to be made are going to be mistakes of the government of Canada for the time being and not the mistakes of Newfoundland, or Alberta, or British Columbia or any of the provincial governments.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: There would not be many mistakes if the provinces have something to do with it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: I am not so sure of that. Even the province of British Columbia makes some mistakes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: "Mistakes" is a mild word.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: It would not bring about good legislation to adopt an amendment of this kind.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was a little surprised to hear the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra make the remark he did. He has sat here for a number of years. I will just use an illustration which everyone here will understand. He is familiar with the C.B.C. How many times has he heard anyone in this house rise and call any particular member of the C.B.C. organization to responsibility? How many times has he seen that happen?
Last spring the hon. member for Peace River very effectively brought before this house an instance of an absolute outrage- a matter involving a play. The name has slipped my memory, but the whole thing was an outrage against the Canadian people and the people of the United States as well. How do we know who it was that made the decision that that play should go on the air? We do not know to this day. Do you think we can find out? How many people have tried to find out? If the hon. member for Peace River had not brought this matter up, how would anyone have learned about it? Let us not imagine that we will be able to pick out individual members of this council and call them to question with regard to mistakes they may have made. But let us remember this: the very nature of the work of the council in the arts, in the humanities and in the sciences, is going to be done in such a way as to permeate and influence the local groups, the schools, and the universities which come under provincial jurisdiction. This is the attitude which the government takes; it is all right for the work of the council to influence provincial education and provincial groups which are concerned with the arts and sciences, but we must not have provincial members appointed to the directorate.

speechtext: I do not want to beg the question and I do not know that it is necessary to write it into the legislation, but to my knowledge we have not yet heard what the salaries of these various officials will be. I hope it is not out of order or repulsive in any way for me to ask that question. Perhaps we could have information as to what it is expected the salaries or remuneration will be for these particular employees, the chairman, vice-chairman, directors and so forth?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
I do not
think it would be appropriate to fix in a definite way in the statute what the salaries would be. I would not expect that for some considerable time there would be other fulltime members of the administration than the director and the assistant director. I would not think the salaries would be large. I do not think those who would be occupying these offices would wish the salaries to be more than what would be apt to cover the expenses that the chairman and vice-chairman will be necessarily incurring in travelling about in the course of the discharge of their duties. I would not expect the salaries would be looked on as other than a sort of honorarium out of which they could provide the necessary expenses that they will incur.
There certainly will be some entertaining it will be appropriate for them to provide, and I do not think they would care to have to make charges for that. If the chairman or vice-chairman were entertaining in Ottawa the president or officers of universities, I do not think they would want to be putting in small chits of that kind for entertainment. I would expect that it would be an honorarium that would be fixed at an amount that would appear to be entirely reasonable under these circumstances. I do not think it would

be appropriate to try to provide the kind of salary for the chairman and vice-chairman that would be their principal source of income because that might be a rather large figure. I feel this would be regarded as a position perhaps comparable to that of the president of a university and certainly the person should be one who would be qualified to occupy that kind of position. I do not think that the salaries should be that kind of a person's chief source of income.

speechtext: There is just a point of clarification here. The clause mentions the chairman, vice-chairman, director and associate director. What is the difference between the functions of the chairman and vice-chairman, and director and associate director?
