subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
I notice in subsection (1) of clause 8, paragraph (a), it says: assist, co-operate with and enlist the aid of organizations, the object of which are similar to any of the objects of the council;
Canada Council
I am particularly glad that this is stated quite definitely in view of the brush I had with my hon. friends to the left this afternoon who were insisting that this was somehow a supergovernment or state culture agency which would not pay too much attention to local organizations in the promotion, as it were, of grass roots efforts. I may say I am just as much interested in the promotion of grass roots efforts as they are. I am glad to see that this is mentioned here specifically.
I have things in mind, of course, and one thinks at once of drama as initiated at Stratford. One thinks too of things like the little theatre in smaller places. I had already mentioned, speaking of my own province although there are lots of things in other provinces of the same nature, the art galleries in Regina. I think this clause is pretty much a refutation of any assertion by anybody that this particular council is going to force upon people some type of culture or something sinister that they do not like. In other words these natural cultures which grow out of the grass roots are going to be encouraged with financial assistance by this council and I think that is desirable.
I just mentioned that in passing, but I do wish to say a word about subsection (2):
The governor in council may assign to the council such functions and duties in relation to the United Nations educational, scientific and cultural organization as he considers desirable.
As the Prime Minister, I even flatter myself, may remember, I have been for some years concerned about the fact-in my opinion it is a fact

that Canada has not been taking advantage of the facilities furnished by this international organization. You will recall, sir, that about 10 years ago, when this organization was set up, Canada was one of the,
I do not know whether enthusiastic signatories, but certainly a signatory, and at the charter meeting I think it was generally understood that the delegates of the nations participating would come back here and initiate the setting up of some sort of national commission. I would suggest, sir, that some of the fear, for example, that has been expressed by my hon. friends that this organization got into the hands of people who they say were subversive or indulged in brain-washing actually came about through ignorance and through non-participation by Canada in that organization. I would suggest to my hon. friends that if they had any suspicion-and no doubt they have-that their assertions are in fact true the proper way to remedy that situation is not to sit on the outside and criticize but to get into the organization and help to make it into the kind of organization they would hope it should be.

Canada Council
As to the object of this particular organization, I, like other Canadians, am not well-informed because we have had no opportunity to take part in its deliberations. I have blamed the government at times for sending to the conference on their own hook, as it were, people who looked as though they were just ad hoc appointments. For the most part they have been civil servants and civil servants from the Department of External Affairs.
I have no fault to find with that because, for various reasons, they would appear to be the appropriate civil servants, but I was not satisfied with that kind of delegation. May I say I have been much more satisfied with the kind of delegation that went last year, and that includes the hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia, who was a member of the group, a man who is eminently qualified by experience and knowledge to participate in this sort of thing.
Now, in regard to this matter of UNESCO, in order that members might inform themselves on some of its functions, its aims and its history, I would like to recommend to hon. members and to the public an article which appeared some time ago in the Queen's Quarterly. The article was reproduced in the paper which I hold in my hand, Canadian Labour, which is an official journal of the Canadian Labour Congress. The article in question was written by Dr. J. R. Kidd and I propose in the few remarks that I hope to make to develop as it were what I have to say from the particular headings that I find in this article.
I can dispose of my hon. friend from Victoria, British Columbia, and get him off my hands, as it were, by quoting a word or two from what he had to say in his very fine speech on January 16, 1957, as recorded in Hansard at pages 306 and 307. I do not know whether the hon. member would go so far as I would go in respect to criticism of his government and say that we have not at the top level taken sufficient interest in this organization. But I noticed several things that my hon. friend said. He said that owing to his visit to this particular conference it had increased his knowledge of other people. Well, sir, I am as loyal and patriotic to my own country as anyone else, but I have a larger patriotism and I am not ashamed to admit it, and that is to the human race. The other thing that the hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia, said and with which I agree is this:
This association is one of the instruments of peace.
That is the second thing. Then, he says something about its reason for existence. He said:

It exists because its members believe that the way to peace is by fostering a more complete understanding of one another, and that this objective can be achieved through education, science and culture.
These last words of his bring us back to the study of the subject with which we are here concerned, namely, this bill which has as its object the promotion of education and of culture. But this organization simply extends what might be a purely national thing into the realm of internationalism with other countries and other peoples.
Let me say at once that while I can sympathize with my hon. friends to my left for being a little nettled, or a little worried that people from other countries of different ideological beliefs which are not the same as our own should be members of that organization,
I do not think you can avoid that. I say that it is a poor principle, a poor doctrine, a poor religion or a poor system of government which cannot stand on its own feet and which cannot stand to be studied and put before the people. If there is something fundamentally wrong about it then the good common sense of the people will reject it, but let us hear all sides of every question. I developed that this afternoon and I shall not weary the committee any further with it. In the article of Dr. Kidd which I propose to analyse briefly, he makes this assertion, and may I say that this article was written some time ago. The pamphlet was put out in December, 1956. He asserts:
But Canada's participation in UNESCO's affairs is still half-hearted.
I have already dealt with that, and I am glad that in the provisions set out here and in this clause of the bill there is some provision by which our participation may be somewhat fuller and more interesting, because there is a provision set out here stating that the council itself or the committee set up by the council may act in lieu or in the place of, if you like, the national commission that the founders of the thing certainly visualized.
There is another thing about this idea that this is some sort of subversive, suspect or sinister organization; and to my hon. friends who are constantly looking for communistic influences I might point out this small quotation from Dr. Kidd's speech or argument, in which he says this:
Canada shares with the Soviet union and three other countries out of 73 member states the distinction of having so far refused to establish some form of commission although the obligation to do so is written into the charter of UNESCO.
I understand that the number of the states has now been increased to 80. This article is perhaps a trifle out of date, but Dr. Kidd stated that 73 was the total, and only five of them, including the Soviet union, with

Canada Council
whom we share the reluctance, have not weary the house by reading all of this mate-joined the organization. One of the accusa- rial because it is set out in detail but I tions that have been brought against this should like to mention one or two things, organization by my hon. friends is that it is The article proceeds to give a little history subversive and yet the communists and the of the organization. It says:
Russian people say it is practically run by the external affairs department of the United States.
Let us look at the men who are interested in this organization and served at the head of it. I wonder if even my hon. friends in the Social Credit party would suggest that the Right Hon. Vincent Massey, Dr. R. C. Wallace, then principal of Queen's University, or Edouard Turcotte, editor of Le Canada are the type of men who would lend their names, their reputations or their assistance to any organization which was subversive?
I do not know how enthusiastic the Prime Minister has been about this organization. I have tried to find out through the years whether he was personally opposed to it or whether there were political or some other influences at work which prevented him from encouraging full participation in this organization. That is not my business and it is not the business of the Prime Minister to tell me. However, I shall quote from a speech he made at the time he endorsed participation by Canada in the organization. He said:
It is desired to have some Canadian body that will be widely representative of the Canadian public and that will be entirely divorced from partisan political influence, to make this a matter in which all those in Canada interested in educational, scientific and cultural developments will feel that they have a part.
Like some of my other dreams of the last 10 or 12 years this is perhaps one of those dreams that is at last coming true and I welcome this clause.

speechtext: What was the date of that?

speechtext:
The speech is on the record. On August 6, 1946 the Prime Minister asked parliament to approve the constitution. He referred to this in his opening speech so I presume this is the approximate date about which my hon. friend is asking.

Many organizations again proposed a commission, and the Massey commission recommended its estabishment as part of the proposed "Canada Council".
That recommendation of the Massey commission has been implemented in this bill. I am not completely clear as to what part the Canada Council is to play in this worldwide organization in spite of the fact that the Prime Minister gave an answer to my question the other day.
There are one or two other things listed under the section that outlines what UNESCO's program involves. I shall not
In its first years, UNESCO's energies were directed toward post-war rehabilitation. In 1948, with Dr. Torres-Bodet of Mexico as director-general, the primary task was a world wide effort to eradicate ignorance and illiteracy.

The article then goes on to discuss general activities and I shall read only one part. It says:
.	.	. promoting understanding of human rights
and international co-operation and research.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I got out a few notes with respect to UNESCO because I thought it would be unfair to leave on the record any impression that we consider it might be a subversive organization. UNESCO is an organization made up I am told of 80 states and has among its active members the United States, all commonwealth countries except the Union of South Africa, all Scandinavian countries and all the countries of western Europe except Portugal. I do not think that that list would indicate that it is a subversive organization.
The director general is Dr. Luther Evans, a United States citizen who before his appointment in 1953 was the librarian of Congress. I am not going to say anything more about him. The assistant directors general are Mr. Rene Maheu, a French national who during the war acted as French liaison officer with the British ministry of education; Mr. Jean Thomas, also a French national, and Mr. Malcom Adiseshia, a national of Ceylon.
I suppose one thing that made some impression on a lot of people was the fact that about three or four years ago the American Legion set up a special committee to investigate UNESCO. The charges that had been made against UNESCO were, first, that it was favourable and tended toward world government by reason of its programs and functions; second, that it was atheistic; and third, that it was communistic or subversive.

That special committee made a very careful and full investigation and reported:
1.	That UNESCO is not favourable toward world government; that the programs and functions of UNESCO are not such as to tend toward world government; that the United States national commission individually and as a group are strongly opposed to world government;
2.	That UNESCO is not atheistic; and
3.	That UNESCO is in no sense or no degree communistic.
The chairman, Mr. Ray Murphy, had this to say:
These conclusions were reached firmly and unanimously by the special committee, not on any cursory basis, but only after the most thorough, exhaustive, time-consuming research, in which the committee, starting from scratch, sought information from any and every available source, pro and con UNESCO.
Notwithstanding that report by its own committee the American Legion refused to accept the report.
At the meeting of July 1956 the executive board of UNESCO rejected a proposal to invite representatives from the following communist countries which are not members of the organization to attend the ninth general conference as observers:
The Republic of China
North Korea
Communist Viet Minh
East Germany
Outer Mongolia
That does not seem to indicate that it was an organization controlled by communist-minded members. In the ten years of its existence UNESCO has facilitated in many ways international co-operation in the fields of education, science and culture. It has done a lot of research work to make regions which were practically non-productive produce crops and thus add to the food stores of the countries interested in those regions, and it has operated very closely in conjunction with FAO.
To promote scientific co-operation UNESCO maintains scientific co-operation offices in Latin America, the Middle East and Asia. Pakistan reported that as a result of UNESCO's assistance in 1950-52 the geophysical observatory at Quetta is now ranked by competent authorities to be one of the finest institutions of its kind in southeast Asia.
UNESCO has established two fundamental education centres, one at Patzcuaro, Mexico, and the other at Sirs-el-Layyan in Egypt. At these centres it trains teachers from countries where illiteracy is a pressing problem. Teachers are enrolled at these centres for eighteen months of training, after which they return to their own countries, I hope better equipped to cope with the problem of extending elementary education.
Canada Council
At the ninth session of the UNESCO conference which concluded recently in New Delhi, India, the conference voted $200,000 for emergency educational relief in Hungary and Egypt. In co-operation with United Nations Relief and Works Agency UNESCO has for the past two years carried on a program for Palestine Arab refugees so that primary education may be available for children and some degree of secondary education as well. UNESCO has proved a valuable agency or exchange bureau for arranging exchanges of scholars in connection with undergraduate and post-graduate work among the countries which are members of the UNESCO organization. Under the charter, the Canada Council cannot itself be the commission, but the charter provides that there shall be national commissions and the implication is that they will not be commissions appointed by the government

that there should be conferences of various kinds of national organizations interested in the work, and that is why this paragraph of section 8 is drawn in its present form. We want to refer to the Canada Council the duty and responsibility of organizing the Canadian conference. These conferences are not conferences of members who are permanently members. Each time one of these conferences is called, ad hoc members are selected by the organizations invited to participate in the conference to come together and deal with an agenda, one of the principal items of which is the selection of delegates to attend the international conference of the central organization.
I think it is unfortunate that there should be any impression that this is an organization with subversive tendencies designed to destroy the patriotism of the populations of the nations that are members of the organization, or that it is atheistic and intended to undermine the respect of children for Christian doctrines or anything of that kind. I think that when anyone looks at the composition of the directorate and of the delegations which attend these conferences, this would certainly not be the impression received. One would hardly get from Mr. Brockington, who led our delegation at New Delhi this year, or from the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) or from the other members of parliament who composed that delegation the reports we did if the organization had any of the dangerous characteristics which some of the hon. gentlemen who spoke this afternoon seemed to think it had. And to suggest that the Canada Council was set up merely to be an agency of UNESCO is to suggest that a pretty short tail would wag the dog.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I said a while ago there were some questions that I wanted

Canada Council
to ask, and there is one matter with regard to which I am not clear.
A great deal of time was spent at university and in college in keeping physically fit, and the games we played-hockey, baseball, boxing, wrestling, skiing and so on-were directed to this end. And I was wondering under what heading these would come-whether it would be under the humanities or the social sciences, because I admit I learned more about humanity and my relations with my fellowmen in some of the games I played than ever I did in studying Latin, Greek or Hebrew and "plugging" to pass examinations.
As I say, I was wondering under what heading these activities would come. Our games have taught us courage-that is what human nature needs-and a definite aim; not to talk all around the thing but to go straight to the point. They taught us patience-and our cabinet ministers have shown me by their conduct, that they have learned something along that line. They taught us determination; when you get the ball under your arm you feel you could go straight through a stone wall in order to make a touchdown. Another thing we learned from our games was to take victory or defeat with grace, and to keep your temper. Everyone knows that when a boxer loses his temper you can lambaste him freely because he can't see straight.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether there is anything in the social sciences or in the humanities which provides for amateurs of athletics in the universities.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
I am afraid, Mr. Chairman, that this does not provide for such encouragement as it might be in the national interest to devote to sports or other athletic activities to which the hon. gentleman has referred. I am not disagreeing with him in his appreciation of the value of these activities, but I do not think I could suggest that they come within the definition of the arts contained in this bill or that they would be included in either of the other two categories, the humanities and the social sciences.
We cannot have too many things in the same basket. It may be we should have at some time an organization that would give attention, for example, to our participation in the Olympic games and to the preparation that should be constantly made so that we would be ready at all times to participate in these games.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
The hon. member for Fort William has introduced an interesting digression into this discussion, and one is tempted to follow this particular approach. I would 
go as far as to say that it is impossible to overestimate the contribution made to national unity by such a sporting event as the Grey Cup final, for example. I recall, too, that we used to have a national physical fitness act, repealed one or two years ago, which tried to do something along those lines.
The contribution I wish to make to the discussion is along the lines followed by the hon. member for Saskatoon. Like him, I am glad to see some specific reference to the agencies which are already operating in the field of the arts, humanities and social sciences. During the discussion of the past day it seemed to me, as I followed it, that there tended to be somewhat of an air of unreality in that a good many hon. members appeared to be under the impression that with the Canada Council we were beginning something that was entirely new-that we were conjuring up activity along cultural lines which was something new in the body politic. Of course, that is far from being the case. We have had a social science research council, we have had a humanities research council, we have had a royal society, a Canada foundation, a Canadian association for adult education, and any number of voluntary organizations which made or are making an outstanding contribution in this field of cultural development.
The question I would like to ask the Prime Minister, Mr. Chairman, is whether he can clarify for the committee in more specific terms the reference under subclause (1) (a) of this section 8 where it says: assist, co-operate with and enlist the aid of organizations, the objects of which are similar to any of the objects of the council
My understanding of the reason for establishing the Canada Council is that its primary function or its primary role will be that of sustaining the activities along these lines already established by the voluntary groups and also providing financial assistance. If that is the case, it would seem to me that the voluntary organizations will still find a useful function in this whole important field of activities. For example, I think the Massey commission on the arts, letters and sciences made a recommendation to the effect that when the Canada Council was established there should be a group of advisory councils to act in an advisory capacity to the Canada Council. Can the Prime Minister indicate to the committee just how the co-operation, the aid and the assistance of the voluntary groups might be called upon in connection with the operation of the Canada Council?
Also, it seems to me that the personnel of the Canada Council, the people making up this important body, is going to determine

to a large degree the success of its operation. It would seem that the men and women who have been providing leadership in the voluntary groups might be the men and women best qualified to provide the leadership that is required in the Canada Council. I have been making one or two suggestions but none of these things are spelled out in detail in subsection (a). I am wondering whether the Prime Minister can tell the committee just how this assistance, co-operation and aid might be asked for.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the section describing the objectives was drawn in general terms so as not to have it exclude anything that it might be found that the body of representative public-spirited Canadians who would constitute the council would feel was something that should be encouraged. How the advisory committees will be organized is to be provided for by bylaws under section 10 of the bill. It was purposely left that way because there was no attempt made to pinpoint the things that might be considered desirable. With the income from the endowment of $50 million, that council will not be able to do all the things that might be desirable. It will have to establish priorities and try to expend the income from the endowment in the manner that it will feel is most apt to impress the public that it is doing the right kind of job.
The hon. gentleman says that those who have led in these movements should be the members of the council. If we were to try to recognize all those who have been effective leaders in the activities contemplated in this statute, we would have to have a council of several hundred persons instead of a council of 19. I do not know of any large town or even any quite small town where there are not some public-spirited citizens who have been influential and beneficial leaders in promoting the kind of activities that are contemplated as being the kind that it would be the duty of the Canada Council to encourage and to assist. There are various activities. I have been asked this question: Will this council be able to provide subsidies for every symphony orchestra throughout the country? I do not know how many there are but I know that there are a great number. It is not always those that are made of the greatest number of musicians which are doing the best work. There are other activities. There are some for whom the ballet is much more important than is a symphony orchestra; there are others who feel quite otherwise about it. In a great many places there are societies that arrange for interesting and instructive
Canada Council
lectures. That may be an activity that will be deserving of some consideration by the Canada Council. I think there will be an ample number of things for them to attend to, even though they will not include the activities that the hon. member for Fort William had in mind. It cannot be denied, however, that there are a great many people who would feel that it would be preferable to encourage sports rather than to encourage symphony orchestras.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: The humanities.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES

I suppose there is the possibility of saying that if sports are not included under the term "the humanities", they should be included. However, there are all these activities. It was intended to try to make this so that it would be the responsibility of the council to decide which were the activities that should get first consideration. The other day I ventured to say that I thought one of the most urgent needs was to assist in the training of a greater number of those who could be the teachers for the increasing numbers who are requiring professors in our institutions of higher learning. That may be at this time something that would be regarded by members of the council as having a high priority in the things to be encouraged. They will know what they can expect as income from the endowment; and I hope they will know what they can expect from the assistance they will get from private citizens or corporations to increase the amounts that will be provided by the income from the endowment, either by adding to the endowment or by making it something to be expended over a short period of time. I think that the possibility of this group being the kind of group that would inspire confidence in those who wanted to be of assistance in that field is a consideration that we shall have to have in mind in making up the council.
I would be sorry if the language used proved to restrict the activities that a properly selected council would find should receive their consideration, their encouragement and assistance. It was to have the language as inclusive in that domain as possible that section 8 setting out the objectives was drawn in these terms which, I confess, are not too precise.

The point in which I was interested was not so much co-operation with the small local groups, such as symphony orchestras or little theatre groups, but rather those organizations such as the large associations on a national scale already operating in this field; the humanities council and the social science council. I am wondering if the

Canada Council
Prime Minister could indicate whether or not there will be some useful function for bodies of that kind under the new Canada Council setup.
Then, just expanding the question for a moment, under paragraph (b), this Canada Council will be providing scholarships and loans to persons in Canada for study or research in the arts, humanities or social sciences. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
There certainly will be a great deal for them to do. For instance, there are some scholarships that are organized under the terms of the instrument setting them up. I was, for a period, a member of the selection committee for the province of Quebec for Rhodes scholarships. This action was taken under the scheme setting up those scholarships, and of course the Canada Council would have no right to interfere. If its assistance were sought, I suppose it would be only too glad to do anything it could to be of assistance. There are scholarships for scientific research that are allocated through the national research council. Some of these blocked funds scholarships are granted, I think, on the recommendation of the Royal Society. I indicated to the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra that I would have no objection to adding to clause 23 his suggestion that would provide that these reports of all the activities of the council, together with the financial statement and report of the Auditor General thereon, would be tabled in parliament. [Mr. Dinsdale.l

speechtext:
The questions I have arise out of the statement the Prime Minister made a few moments ago when replying to the thought that was expressed by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris. The fact is that we in this group have indicated we were quite prepared to accept the use of some of these funds-in fact, we had hoped all of it would be channelled through organizations that are in operation, provincial bodies that are set up, thus giving us more money for the purpose for which this was apparently intended. However, I believe the Prime Minister indicated that the revenue from the $50 million would be quite small and that priorities would have to be set up. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Of course, if parliament at any future time saw fit to add to the original endowment of $50 million, parliament would then determine how much it would be and how it would be used. If individuals or corporations choose to make any gifts either by acts inter vivos or as to individual, by testamentary disposition, they will have the right to determine in the document' making the conveyance the conditions that they wish to attach to their gifts. They could make a gift to the university capital grants fund or they could make a gift to the endowment fund and determine, in the instruments evidencing the gift, the conditions that they wished to impose.
As to what portion of the income could be devoted to activities outside of Canada, I would imagine-and that was the intention in setting up the bill-that it would be merely on the basis of reciprocal exchanges that they could arrange for scholarships in Canada for people coming from elsewhere; but that they would try to negotiate in such a way that it would be an exchange, and that Canadian

graduates, or perhaps even undergraduates, would get an equivalent benefit in the country from which others came to Canada.
It is not intended in a general way to make this a supplement to what parliament votes for the Colombo plan or what parliament votes as its contribution to the United Nations or anything of that kind. This is intended to be something to foster the development of the arts, the humanities and the social sciences in Canada. That can be done possibly to a certain extent by studies made by Canadians elsewhere in exchange for scholarships established here for persons coming from outside. This is intended to be something set up to improve the situation for Canadians.

provide, through appropriate organization . . .

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just before we go any farther with this clause, I should like to make one or two comments on what was said just a little while ago. The hon. member for Saskatoon did extol some of the virtues of UNESCO by depicting some of the things which it had done. He did so as he spoke in
Canada Council
apposition to the position which this group takes. Now, Mr. Chairman, I am quite prepared to admit that in some branches UNESCO has done some good work throughout the world, and some of those branches are the ones which the hon. member for Saskatoon put on the record; but there is another branch in which we think that UNESCO has played a very sinister part, and we have already placed on the record our belief in respect of that.
I should like to call the Prime Minister's attention to something. He also rose in defence of UNESCO and stated that much of the criticism that has arisen was by reason of some action that was taken by the American legion; that there was a feeling among those members of the American legion that UNESCO was contrary, or working in opposition, to the best interests of the United States.
The Prime Minister said that as a result of that suspicion the American legion brought into existence a committee to investigate whether or not UNESCO was in any sense sinister to United States interest and to the United States way of life, and that the committee had reported they could find nothing that would indicate or verify their suspicions. I think the Prime Minister said that that committee of the legion reported two or three years ago. He did not give the date, but let me say this: the Prime Minister is just a little bit behind the times. In saying that, the Prime Minister appeared to wipe the slate completely clean and therefore give UNESCO a completely clean slate. I say once again that the Prime Minister is a little bit behind the times because, on March 7, 1956, the commander of the American legion appeared before a subcommittee on international organizations and movements of the house committee on foreign affairs of the United States congress. He appeared there to present to that subcommittee a resolution that was passed by the American legion as late as October, 1955. That is less than 18 months ago. Commander J. Addington Wagner, head of the legion, appeared before this subcommittee of congress as late as March 7, 1956, which is less than a year ago. He placed on the record a resolution passed by the American legion convention.
I am not going to read the entire resolution, but I will read enough of it to indicate what it is all about. This matter was introduced in a speech in congress by the Hon. H. R. Gross of Iowa, the day after Commander Wagner had made his statement.

Canada Council
This is what he says concerning the committee that the Prime Minister referred to a little while ago:
Mr. Wagner also effectively explodes the widely circulated myth that UNESCO was tried by the legion in a star chamber proceeding, and that the legion's stand did not reflect the judgment of a majority of legionnaires.
The commander exploded the myth that the Prime Minister brought up this evening.
Now then, when he made this submission to that sub-committee he presented the legion's resolution and I shall read the pertinent part of it:
Resolved, that the American Legion urges Congress to repeal the laws creating the United States National Commission for UNESCO and its Secretariat; and that Congress deliver mandates to all administrative departments of the United States government to desist from further dissemination of UNESCO and United States National Commission for UNESCO materials, reports, and programs within the territorial jurisdiction of the United States.
That was done as late as March 1956. The rest of the resolution urges congress to make a complete current investigation of the operations of UNESCO in order to determine whether or not that agency has complied with its terms of reference.
In the light of that it is small wonder that we are suspicious and we cannot wipe the slate clean by referring to a previous committee of the legion. This gives us reason for fear. As I put on the record the other day, the state of Texas investigated this matter because of indignation that was aroused among the people of that state in respect of the influence of UNESCO upon their educational institutions. I also placed on the record what occurred in Pasadena and Los Angeles where through the indignation of the people a committee of the state legislature of California was set up to investigate the whole matter. In their report the committee stated that the UNESCO material that was infiltrating their educational institutions was detrimental to the United States of America. In the light of all these things it is no wonder that we have some fear when we discover that this council is to be tied to UNESCO. I shall say no more at the moment about our fears. As I said the other day I hope that they will prove to be wrong; I sincerely hope that. It is my earnest hope that this council will perform a great and valuable work for Canada and the world but because we know what has taken place we warn that all may not go well in the years to come.
Perhaps I may be permitted to say this, Mr. Chairman. I know we will not defeat the bill. I know that the council will be established. If the opposition we in this group have demonstrated does nothing more

than warn the people of Canada against any possible sinister influences that might be the result of the work of this council, then what we have done will have served a good purpose.

One thing which particularly interests me is this. I simply want to put one sentence on the record because it describes the objects of UNESCO. It seems to me we have to keep our feet on the ground and understand the purpose of the organization which we are discussing. In the official publication of the United Nations entitled "Everyman's United Nations" under the heading of UNESCO the following words appear:
The purpose of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, as defined in its Constitution, is to "contribute to peace and security by promoting collaboration among the nations through education, science and culture in order to further universal respect for justice, for the rule of law, and for the human rights and fundamental freedoms for all," . . .
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that these are objects which should be sought by all Canadian citizens. I think the type of remarks that have been directed toward UNESCO during the course of this debate indicates

a feverish desire on the part of UNESCO detractors to sow seeds of suspicion in this country concerning an organization which has such worthy objectives that they should be shared by all people throughout the world.
There is one question I should like to ask the Prime Minister. After the setting up of the Canada Council is it the intention of the government to invoke clause 27 of the UNESCO charter and seek from that organization a member of its secretariat to serve either as a permanent or part-time member of the Canada Council?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, it is not the intention to ask UNESCO to appoint a member of the council any more than it would be our intention to have any of the members appointed by a Canadian provincial government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I could ask the Prime Minister whether in view of the need to co-ordinate the activities of the various national commissions of UNESCO he might not feel such a move would be a good one in that connection?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: No, I think not, Mr. Chairman. We want to keep this a Canadian council and if the council requires advice from any source outside of Canada it will be able to obtain that advice. We think of it as a council composed of Canadians that should have the responsibility for making the decisions.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have just one question which may have been asked while I was unavoidably absent from the chamber. Would it be within the powers of this council to accept donations for specific purposes? For example, if a family, a firm or an organization wished to endow a scholarship for a particular purpose or if they wished to endow a scholarship to commemorate the memory of some individual, could that be done through this council? I would also like to know if it would be feasible to link the scholarships with the names of war veterans so as at the same time to have them serve as a sort of war memorial? I understand that as time goes on the funds at the disposal of this council will probably increase considerably, which would perhaps make this possible.

There was a donation made by a family in Ontario to the University of Toronto to establish lectures as a tribute to the memory

I think it would be quite proper if a Canadian wished to have something within the scope of the normal activities of the Canada Council provided for out of income or capital of a donation to do that and to have it published that it was done as a memorial to such and such a person or of such and such an event that was of special interest to the donor of the funds required to carry out that purpose.

Mr. Chairman, there are several matters which I think it would be fitting to bring to the attention of the committee at this stage. The first meeting of the United States national commission for UNESCO was held in Washington on September 23, 1946, with Senator William Benton of Connecticut as the chairman. On that occasion Senator Benton said:
We are at the beginning of a long process of breaking down the walls of national sovereignty. In this process UNESCO must be the pioneer. The department of state has fathered this national commission (for UNESCO) . . .
Senator Benton's remarks may be found in state department publication 2726 of United Nations information, series No. 14. The question which hon. members like the hon. member for Regina City need to ask themselves and answer is: Why should Senator Benton express the objectives of UNESCO which he expressed, and why should some corresponding figure in Canada express any other objective? It needs explaining. The hon. member quoted a passage from article I of the constitution of UNESCO, and the quotation I am about to give includes the words read by the hon. member for Regina City:
The purpose of the organization is to contribute to peace and security by promoting collaboration among the nations through education, science and culture in order to further universal respect for justice, for the rule of law and for the human rights and fundamental freedoms which are affirmed for the peoples of the world, without distinction of race, sex, language or religion, by the charter of the United Nations.
That passage will be found in basic documents of UNESCO, page 8.
The ideals which are expressed by the UNESCO enthusiasts are just so beautiful that one almost feels he has drifted away into celestial regions, but the all-important question we have to ask ourselves is by what means is it proposed that these laudable objectives shall be achieved? When we come to answer that question and probe into the details of the problem we find an altogether different appearance on the inside of the cup from that which we see on the outside of the cup looking so shiny and clean.

Canada Council
After that rather promising suggestion, what do we find after ten years of development of UNESCO effort in the United States? I can hear the hon. member for Regina City say, "Oh, well, we are going to be different in Canada." I know we are, but we had better be warned by what has happened in the United States because in a general way we are very much the same kind of people. We are deluded by the same kind of things that delude them. Here are some indications of what was stated positively not so very long ago in a book which I think is authentic. It is said that UNESCO is trying so hard to destroy American patriotism.

After his sub-committee held hearings on UNESCO Senator Pat McCarran had this to say:	These are Senator McCarran's
words, and I quote:
This is a very clever propaganda campaign to sell the people of this country and particularly the school children on the doctrine of one world government and world citizenship. The committee had presented to it documented proof of this insidious campaign.
As a reference I direct my hon. friends to the departments of state, justice and commerce and judiciary appropriations for 1953- the hearings before a subcommittee of the committee of appropriations of the United States senate, 82nd Congress H. R. 7289, page 1514-1534. Maybe that is accurate enough information.
General Sumter L. Lorry, retired, speaking before that United States subcommittee, as reported on page 1516, used the following words, and I quote:
The state department's prime concern for existence is to protect and preserve the interests of the United States yet that same state department is taking taxpayers' money and using it to create a world government to replace our own. By no possible reasoning should the state department be

engaged in any effort which, if carried to a conclusion, would destroy our country and American institutions.
There will be those who will say: "We have not the facilities to go and see those originals for ourselves". To them, may I give the means whereby they may check the accuracy of the record. They may do so by referring to an article entitled: "UNESCO-Greatest Danger to American Youth and Schools." This article is the major article in the February 1, 1957, issue of the well-known political journal Common Sense, founded and edited by that great and courageous Christian fighter Conde McGinley.
There is much more that could be said, but I think those three quotations strike with the blow of a sledgehammer. You could hardly find any more dependable quotations. Senator McCarran is famous all over the world for his investigations; he was the chairman of the McCarran committee for years-the man who uncovered more subversion and danger in the United States than, probably, any other man in this country. No one could question what he might say at the conclusion of an investigation especially directed to UNESCO. I will not say that General Lorry is necessarily a great authority, but he was invited by Senator Pat McCarran's committee to give evidence.
Now, Mr. Chairman, may I point out just three or four things? The first quotation I gave from Lillian Moon Robert's establishes, if we can accept her evidence-and all the other quotations tend to support her-that what the Prime Minister considers so regrettable, namely, that the idea should go abroad that UNESCO was trying to destroy the faith of the child in its parents, that UNESCO was trying to destroy the faith of the child in religion, that' UNESCO was trying to destroy the faith of the child in its country-to destroy patriotism-is actually the situation today. It is all established there. It has been proved in Texas and in California.
Let no hon. member go running off with the idea that the Social Credit position has been lightly taken. We have been following this matter for a good many years, keeping ourselves quite as well informed as any of our companion groups in this house, I believe, and I think a perusal of the speeches we have made and a study of the attitudes we have taken all the way through will tend to support what I have said.
People will say: "Why would they want to destroy patriotism?" Because in every country which is a democracy the only thing that holds people together as a unit is patriotism, love of country. In a dictatorship such as those of Russia and China, the things that hold people together are force and fear. Now, if they can destroy this cement of patriotism which binds individual Americans
Canada Council
together, which binds individual Canadians together, then the people will be just as helpless as a flock of sheep without a shepherd in a storm; they will stray all over the place and be easy prey for the wolves of international revolution who are working all over this world as a group, and who have accomplished results of appalling magnitude and success in an appallingly short time. Surely, Mr. Chairman, we cannot afford to take any chances!
Why do they want to destroy faith in God? Because the one thing that binds all Christians together is belief in the Bible, and if belief in the Bible can be destroyed, then once more the solidarity of religion will be destroyed. The other great binding force which might hold men together in the fearful struggle that lies before us in the next ten years will have been annihilated and once more the free people will be adrift and lost- the easiest kind of prey for the manipulators who are working continually on world revolution with the definite objective of bringing about a complete world dictatorship under the control of a few international tricksters and masterminds.
Why do they want to destroy reverence for the mother and father? One reason that comes to my mind is that one of the Ten Commandments is: "Honour thy father and thy mother that thy days may be long upon the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee". And if you cease to honour your father and mother, you are preparing to lose that land, and that is what these international monopolists want-they want to lay their hands on every land that the free peoples have.
Now I move, Mr. Chairman, that we rise and report progress.
